label: The Tychonoff Theorem
notes: Open the chapter, which spans printed pages 228 through 240. The Tychonoff theorem asserts that an arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology. It is one of the most important and surprising theorems of topology, equivalent to the axiom of choice, with deep consequences across analysis and logic.

label: Statement
notes: The theorem states that the product of any family of compact topological spaces, indexed by an arbitrary set, is compact. The subtlety lies in the infinite case, where the product topology uses only finitely many constraints. This restraint is exactly what makes compactness survive into arbitrary products.

label: Finite Products
notes: For finitely many factors, compactness of the product follows from the tube lemma applied repeatedly. Given an open cover, one covers each slice by finitely many basic open sets and assembles a finite subcover. The genuine difficulty appears only when infinitely many factors must be handled simultaneously.

label: Arbitrary Products
notes: The general proof uses the finite intersection property: a space is compact when every collection of closed sets with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection. One extends a family to a maximal one using Zorn's lemma, then projects to find a point lying in the closure of every set.

label: Choice and Equivalence
notes: The Tychonoff theorem is logically equivalent to the axiom of choice; choosing a point of the product is choosing one coordinate from each factor. This is why the proof invokes Zorn's lemma or the well-ordering theorem. The theorem thus sits exactly at the level of choice in the foundations of mathematics.

label: Applications
notes: Tychonoff's theorem underlies the Stone-Cech compactification, the construction of the space of probability measures, and compactness arguments in functional analysis like the Banach-Alaoglu theorem. It is the workhorse that lets infinite-dimensional and product constructions retain compactness. Next: metrization theorems and paracompactness.
